# The Department of Unfinished Things

On her first morning at the Department of Unfinished Things, Mara was given a desk, a brass key, and a sandwich wrapped in yesterday’s newspaper.

“The desk is yours,” said Mr. Vale. “The key is communal. The sandwich belongs to someone who never came back from lunch.”

“How long ago?”

“Tuesday.”

It was Thursday. Mara set the sandwich aside.

Mr. Vale looked relieved. Apparently this had been a test, although she could not tell whether she had passed.

The department occupied the upper three floors of a building that appeared, from the street, to have only two. Visitors generally arrived by accident. They took the stairs looking for a dentist, or followed the smell of coffee through a door marked ELECTRICAL, and emerged among the filing cabinets with an expression Mara would soon recognize: embarrassment complicated by hope.

Her job was to receive their unfinished things.

Not objects, exactly. Objects could be donated elsewhere. The department accepted what remained attached to them.

A woman brought the first chapter of a novel and the seventeen years during which she had meant to write the second. A retired electrician delivered an apology, folded so often that it had become soft as cloth. A boy arrived carrying an empty aquarium.

“The fish died,” he explained.

“We don’t generally handle bereavement,” Mr. Vale said gently.

“I know. But I was going to teach it a trick.”

They accepted the aquarium.

***

The work was less sorrowful than Mara had expected.

There were unfinished feuds, which arrived hot and had to be handled with tongs. There were abandoned diets, mostly harmless, though one spent a week whispering insults from a biscuit tin. A proposed opera about municipal drainage occupied a cupboard and occasionally produced a tremendous chord.

Then there were the unfinished conversations.

These were stored in glass jars, each labeled with a date and the words that had actually been spoken. Mara learned never to open one without first reading the label.

WELL, IF THAT’S WHAT YOU THINK contained thirty years of marriage.

DID YOU GET HOME ALL RIGHT? contained a love affair that neither participant had recognized.

One tiny jar, scarcely bigger than a thimble, was labeled DAD?

Mr. Vale caught her looking at it.

“Some things take up less room than they should,” he said.

He was an elderly man with impeccable cuffs and the distracted manner of someone listening for a kettle in another building. He had worked at the department for forty-three years. Before that, he said, he had intended to become an architect.

“What happened?”

He tapped the desk between them.

Mara thought he meant that the job had happened. Later, opening the wrong drawer, she found a small white city beneath a blue sky. Its streets smelled of rain. Tiny trams moved between buildings whose windows caught the light.

She shut the drawer carefully.

Her own unfinished thing was at home, in a green envelope beneath a stack of takeaway menus.

It was a letter to her younger brother, Daniel.

They had not spoken in six years.

People assumed there must have been an argument of corresponding size: an inheritance, a betrayal, an unforgivable sentence delivered at a funeral. In fact, the original argument had concerned a ladder.

Their mother had needed her gutters cleared. Daniel had promised to do it. He had forgotten. Mara had done it herself, fallen from the third rung, and broken her wrist.

When Daniel called, she said he always left her to deal with things.

He said she never let anyone forget a mistake.

Both statements had sufficient truth in them to do damage.

Afterward, each waited for the other to become a different sort of person.

Their mother died eighteen months later. They managed the funeral with the brittle politeness of strangers sharing a railway compartment. Daniel took the photographs. Mara took the crockery. Neither asked whether the other had wanted something else.

The letter began: I don’t think either of us meant for this to last so long.

She had written that sentence three years ago.

At the department, she became particularly efficient with unfinished correspondence. She could sort a hundred letters in an hour, arranging them by recipient, urgency, and likelihood of containing money.

She did not bring in her own.

***

In November, the city announced an inspection.

The notice arrived on thick paper and contained the phrases asset utilization, legacy provision, and measurable public benefit.

Mr. Vale read it twice.

“They mean to close us,” he said.

“Does it say that?”

“Not yet. First they ask us to explain why we exist. Then they discover that our explanation doesn’t fit in the box.”

For a week, they prepared.

Mara counted unmade journeys. Mr. Vale checked the seals on the conversations. Together they moved a stalled revolution away from a radiator.

The inspector arrived on a wet Monday. Her name was Mrs. Bell, and she wore sensible shoes. Mara had expected someone sharp and bloodless, but Mrs. Bell looked tired. She accepted tea and took a biscuit without apologizing for it.

“How many cases do you resolve annually?” she asked.

“Resolve?” said Mr. Vale.

“Complete. Return to use. Dispose of satisfactorily.”

“We preserve them.”

“Yes. I understand the storage function.”

“It isn’t simply storage.”

Mrs. Bell waited.

Mr. Vale described the aquarium. He showed her a half-knitted cardigan that was still warm from the lap of the woman who had started it. He opened a box containing someone’s intention to learn the names of trees.

Mrs. Bell touched a paper leaf.

“My husband used to know them,” she said.

Then she withdrew her hand and returned to her forms.

“What happens if these things remain unfinished?”

“Usually,” Mr. Vale said, “they remain here.”

“For how long?”

He looked toward the cabinets.

The inspection lasted four hours. At its conclusion, Mrs. Bell gave them thirty days to demonstrate a viable completion pathway for the collection.

Otherwise, the department would be consolidated.

“Into what?” Mara asked.

“That hasn’t been determined.”

After she left, Mr. Vale sat very still.

Mara began gathering the teacups. Behind her, the drainage opera sounded a muted, apprehensive note.

For the first time, the department seemed less like a refuge than a place where things had been left because leaving them was easier.

***

That evening, Mara took the green envelope out from beneath the menus.

She read her sentence.

Then she wrote another.

I still think you should have done the gutters.

She stared at it, appalled, and began to laugh.

The laugh was unpleasant at first, almost a cough. Then it loosened something. She laughed until her eyes watered, alone at the kitchen table, with the letter in front of her and a cold cup of tea beside her elbow.

She crossed out the new sentence.

Then she uncrossed it, as far as that was possible.

She added: But I probably didn’t need to make it a theory of your entire character.

By midnight she had written four pages. Three were explanations of why she had been right. She put those in the recycling.

The remaining page was awkward and incomplete. It said she missed him. It asked whether he still lived at the same address, which was not a useful question to put inside a letter sent to that address.

She posted it anyway.

The next morning she asked Mr. Vale whether anyone ever came back for something.

“Occasionally.”

“What do we do?”

“Locate the item. Verify ownership. Obtain a signature.”

“Could we invite them?”

He removed his glasses.

“Some people have entrusted us with things they cannot bear.”

“Some people may have forgotten where they put them.”

“And you propose to remind them?”

“I propose to ask.”

They argued until lunchtime. It was their first argument, and Mara was surprised by how much she disliked seeing him unhappy. He was surprised, apparently, that she could disagree without preparing to leave.

Finally, he unlocked a cabinet marked OUTREACH.

Inside was a telephone directory, a box of stamps, and a proposal dated thirty-one years earlier.

The proposal was his.

“I couldn’t decide how to phrase the invitation,” he said.

They used the paper from the back of it.

***

The invitations were brief.

*You left something with us.*

*You do not have to finish it.*

*You are welcome to come and decide what should happen to it next.*

Mara insisted on the middle sentence. Mr. Vale insisted on adding the opening hours.

They sent two hundred invitations before running out of stamps.

On Saturday, eleven people came.

The novelist arrived first. She was older than Mara expected, brisk and well dressed, with a shopping bag containing leeks.

“I don’t want to write it,” she said, as soon as Mara produced the manuscript.

“That’s allowed.”

“I wanted to have written it. That’s quite different.”

She read the first page, smiled at something, and asked for a pencil. For twenty minutes she made small corrections. Then she folded the pages and put them beside the leeks.

“My granddaughter likes stories,” she said. “Perhaps she’ll enjoy how dreadful this is.”

The retired electrician took his apology away unopened.

The aquarium boy returned with his father. He had grown tall enough that Mara barely recognized him.

“I thought it might be for another fish,” he said. “But I don’t really want another fish.”

They discussed it seriously. Eventually he decided to grow something in the tank.

Mr. Vale found a packet of seeds in an abandoned plan for self-sufficiency.

Other visits went less well.

A woman came for a conversation with her sister, listened to three words, and asked them to put it back. A man accused the department of stealing his youth. Someone opened a failed business proposal and immediately tried to borrow money from the electrician.

By four o’clock, Mara had a headache.

“This isn’t much of a completion pathway,” she admitted.

Mr. Vale was sweeping soil from beneath the reception desk.

“No,” he said. “But it’s considerably more interesting than counting.”

Near closing time, Mrs. Bell appeared.

She stood in the doorway, holding one of their invitations.

“I didn’t send you one,” Mara said.

“I know.”

The paper was old and yellow, with a different letterhead. Mrs. Bell smoothed it against her coat.

“My husband brought something here. Years ago. I found the receipt.”

Mr. Vale took it from her.

He read the number and went upstairs without speaking.

While they waited, Mrs. Bell explained that her husband had planned to build a boat. Not a large boat. Something wooden, with a little sail.

“He bought books. Measured the garage. Talked about it every winter.”

“What stopped him?”

“The usual things. Work. Children. Then his hands.”

Mr. Vale returned carrying a shallow wooden tray. Inside lay a stretch of water beneath an evening sky. A small boat rested against a jetty. Its sail was furled.

Mrs. Bell put her fingers to her mouth.

For a long time, nobody said anything.

“Can I?” she asked.

Mr. Vale nodded.

She touched the boat with one finger. It rocked, making a quiet wooden sound against the jetty.

“He would have loved that,” she said.

Then, after a moment: “I wouldn’t. I get terribly seasick.”

She laughed once, and wiped her face with the heel of her hand.

She did not take the tray home. Instead, she asked whether someone else might want it.

***

Daniel’s reply arrived on a Wednesday.

It was a postcard showing a lighthouse neither of them had visited.

On the back he had written:

*I absolutely should have done the gutters.*

*I’m free Sunday.*

Mara carried it in her pocket all day. Twice she took it out to verify that the words had not changed.

Sunday was not a reconciliation of the sort people describe afterward as inevitable. Daniel arrived late. Mara had chosen a café he disliked, having forgotten that he disliked it. They hugged with their shoulders rather than their arms.

For the first ten minutes they discussed parking.

Then Daniel asked about her wrist.

“It’s fine.”

“Does it hurt when it’s cold?”

“Sometimes.”

He nodded. She watched him turn his cup by the handle. His hair was thinner. There was a small scar on his chin she didn’t remember.

“I missed quite a lot,” she said.

“Me too.”

They talked for an hour. Their mother came into the conversation and stayed there. Daniel remembered things Mara had forgotten; Mara corrected him twice and managed not to correct him a third time.

When they left, nothing had been settled about who had done more or cared more or suffered more.

But Daniel had offered to bring the photographs next Sunday.

Mara had said she would cook.

At work, the thirty days passed.

Mrs. Bell submitted a report recommending that the department remain open for a six-month trial, with revised procedures and quarterly reviews.

Mr. Vale complained about the quarterly reviews for an entire afternoon. Then he went out and bought better tea.

They changed the forms. After NAME and DESCRIPTION, Mara added WHAT WOULD YOU LIKE US TO DO WITH IT? There were four boxes: KEEP, RETURN, OFFER TO SOMEONE ELSE, and I DON’T KNOW YET.

Most people ticked the fourth.

The new arrangements did not empty the department. By spring, they needed another cabinet. But things moved now. A teacher took the proposed boat to a school beside the reservoir. The drainage opera found a brass band willing to attempt its overture. The electrician came back to say that his apology had not been accepted, but he was glad to have delivered it.

Mr. Vale began taking Fridays off.

In the drawer beneath his desk, the small white city acquired a railway station. Later, a park appeared beside it, with benches positioned where afternoon sunlight would fall.

One evening, Mara found him studying a blank patch beyond the tiny river.

“Another building?” she asked.

“Possibly.”

“What kind?”

“I haven’t decided.”

He closed the drawer, put on his coat, and turned off the lamp.

Downstairs, someone was waiting on the landing with a parcel.

Mara opened the door.

“Am I too late?” the visitor asked.

She glanced at Mr. Vale. He shrugged and took off his coat again.

“Not tonight,” she said. “Come in. What have you brought?”
